client: I've been really struggling since last week's team meeting at work. My colleague called out some mistakes I made in front of everyone, and I just can't stop replaying it in my head. I'm already feeling overwhelmed by all the demands of this new job, and now I'm starting to wonder if I'm even cut out for it — honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: What you went through in that meeting sounds genuinely painful — being called out in front of others can feel humiliating, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps returning to it. I also notice you came here even while doubting it would help, and I think that took real courage. Can you tell me a little more about what that voice in your head keeps saying when you replay the moment — what's the story it's telling you about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It keeps saying that everyone in that room now sees me as incompetent, like I've permanently damaged how they think of me. And the worst part is my manager was there, so I can't stop thinking that my whole career there might be over because of one mistake I made in that presentation. It's like my brain won't let me move past it — I just keep replaying the moment he interrupted me and corrected me in front of everyone, and each time it feels just as awful as when it actually happened.
therapist: That sounds exhausting — like your mind has turned that one moment into a verdict about your entire worth and future there, which is such a heavy thing to carry. The way you're describing it, one mistake has become evidence of permanent, irreversible damage, and I'm curious — if a trusted friend had made that same error in a meeting, would you see *their* whole career as over? What would you tell them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't tell a friend their career was over. I'd probably say it was just one bad moment and people forget these things. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm being held to this impossible standard that I can't even explain, and telling myself what I'd tell a friend just feels hollow, like I know the "right" answer but it doesn't actually land emotionally.
therapist: You've actually just named something really important — that knowing the "right" answer and *feeling* it are two very different things, and that gap is exactly where a lot of our work can happen. It sounds like there's a part of you that holds yourself to a standard you'd never apply to someone you care about, and I'm wondering — where do you think that impossible standard comes from for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's... actually a really hard question to sit with. therapist: What you just shared is profound, and it takes real courage to trace it back that far — that belief that you have to *earn* your right to exist in a space is such a heavy thing to have carried, probably for most of your life. I notice you said it quite quickly, like the words came out in a rush, and I want to make sure we don't move past it too fast — can you sit with that for a moment and tell me what it feels like to say that out loud?

client: Yeah, I... okay. Sitting with it feels uncomfortable, honestly, like I said something I wasn't supposed to say out loud. It's weird because part of me wants to take it back or laugh it off, but I also know it's true — I've always felt like I need to justify why I'm taking up space, whether that's at work, with friends, even just in a room.
therapist: That urge to take it back or laugh it off makes complete sense — when we say something true that we've never quite let ourselves fully acknowledge, it can feel almost like a betrayal of a very old, protective part of ourselves. And yet you didn't take it back, you stayed with it, and that matters. I'm curious — what would it mean for you, even just as a small possibility, if you were allowed to take up space simply because you exist, without having to justify it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think if I'm really honest, I'm not sure I've ever actually believed that was allowed for me, and I don't know if I can just decide to believe it now because it sounds like a good idea in theory.
therapist: You're absolutely right that you can't just *decide* to believe it because it sounds good — that's not how deeply held beliefs work, and it would feel hollow to pretend otherwise. But I want to gently reflect something back: the fact that a part of you can even recognize that unconditional belonging *sounds* nice suggests that somewhere, however faintly, a part of you can imagine it being real. What do you think that part of you needs — not to fully believe it yet, but just to feel a little safer exploring it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... that part of me needs some kind of evidence, maybe? Like, not just words or reassurances, but something that actually shows me I belong somewhere before I can even start to believe it. therapist: What you just said — that you might not even recognize the evidence if it showed up — feels like one of the most important things you've shared today, because it points to something really worth exploring: that the filter through which you've learned to see yourself might be screening out the very proof you're looking for. And I notice you said all of that quite quickly, like the words were tumbling out — I wonder if there's something about saying it that feels urgent, or even a little frightening. What would it mean if the evidence has actually been there at times, but something inside you has made it hard to let it in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think... yeah, it does feel a little frightening to say out loud. Like if I admit that maybe the evidence has been there and I've just been blocking it out, then I have to take some responsibility for how isolated I've made myself feel, and that's a really uncomfortable thought. It's easier to believe no one's ever really shown up for me than to consider that maybe I've been pushing things away without realizing it.
therapist: The honesty it takes to say that out loud is remarkable — recognizing that we might have had a hand in our own pain is one of the hardest things a person can do, and it's actually a sign of real growth, not something to punish yourself for. That discomfort you're feeling isn't a verdict against you; it's the feeling of something important shifting. I'm wondering — if you could approach that realization with even a little compassion for the younger version of you who learned to push things away as a way of protecting yourself, what would you want to say to them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know... part of me wants to say something kind to that younger version of me, but another part feels like that would just be making excuses for why I kept people at arm's length for so long. Like, if I'm too understanding with myself, I'm just letting myself off the hook for the loneliness I've caused. It's hard to separate "having compassion" from "avoiding accountability."
therapist: What you're describing — that fear that compassion equals letting yourself off the hook — is actually one of the most common ways our inner critic keeps us stuck, because it disguises itself as accountability when it's really just more punishment. But here's something worth sitting with: true accountability is about understanding how something happened so you can do differently, and you can't really do that while you're still beating yourself up. I notice something quieter in how you're holding all of this right now — like it's landing somewhere deep — and I'm curious, do you think the loneliness you've carried has actually been *solved* by being hard on yourself, or has that harshness always just kept you company in it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
